slides.narration: The learning target is not memorizing an algorithm name. Learners should be able to explain why the algorithm is correct, what input size or structure controls cost, and what output or trace proves the implementation followed the intended procedure. question.prompt: Why is passing one test not the same as proving an algorithm?
question.answer: A test samples behavior. A proof or invariant explains why the procedure works for the stated input domain; tests then serve as witnesses and regression guards.

slides.title: 11.2.1 Understanding AVL Rotations
keyPoints: For a right rotation, call the old root y, its left child x, and x’s right subtree B.
Before the rotation, every key in B is greater than x and less than y.
Promote x, make B the new left subtree of y, and attach y as x’s right child.
The ordering of A, x, B, y, C is unchanged.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 11, treat 11.2.1 Understanding AVL Rotations as an algorithmic claim. For a right rotation, call the old root y, its left child x, and x’s right subtree B. Before the rotation, every key in B is greater than x and less than y. Promote x, make B the new left subtree of y, and attach y as x’s right child. The ordering of A, x, B, y, C is unchanged. Update the demoted node’s height before the promoted node’s height because the latter depends on the former. A left-left insertion is repaired by one right rotation. A right-right insertion is symmetric. For left-right, rotate the left child left and then rotate the root right; right-left uses the opposite pair. The tests use the three-key insertion orders 3,2,1; 1,2,3; 3,1,2; and 1,3,2 so each branch is deliberately exercised. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran.
